title: The Barkley Marathons
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the show's producer-style banter) cover the Barkley Marathons, the notoriously brutal ultra-distance trail race held at Frozen Head State Park in northeastern Tennessee. They trace its origins to Gary Cantrell (Lazarus Lake) and his friend Carl Hen (Raw Dog), the 1977 escape of James Earl Ray from Brushy Mountain State Penitentiary that inspired the race, the first 1986 edition, the race format (loops, time limits, elevation, route, no GPS), the application process, the start with a cigarette, the Fun Run designation, the book-page checkpoint system, the taps and "That was easy" button, record finishers and the 2025-era record and first female finisher, and a listener email on the difference between a lake and a pond.

segments.title: Opening and Chad's suggestion
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, which came from producer friend Chad Crowley's ultramarathon running, and recommend the documentary about the Barkley Marathons.

segments.title: Documentary and banter on prior marathon episodes
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the 2017 documentary about the race and its hardness, then briefly joke about a past marathon episode and a Saturn's rings short.
topics: The Race That Eats Its Young

segments.title: Gary Cantrell and the race's origin name
segments.summary: Gary Cantrell (Lazarus Lake) is introduced as the creator, named after farmer Barry Barkley. His background as a runner, smoker, and Boy Scout who discovered endurance is described.

segments.title: Ultramarathon origins and Tennessee journey runs
segments.summary: Cantrell started ultra running in the 1970s, and as the ultra craze began with the Western States 100 in 1974, he began organizing his own Tennessee races, including journey runs, the Volunteer State Road Race, and the Idiots Run.

segments.title: Location: Frozen Head State Park and region
segments.summary: The race is held at Frozen Head State Park in the Cumberland Mountains of northeastern Tennessee, a remote, harsh area surrounded by about 24,000 acres of forest, with a history tied to convict leasing and coal mining.

segments.title: Brushy Mountain prison and James Earl Ray inspiration
segments.summary: The history of Brushy Mountain State Penitentiary and the 1977 escape of James Earl Ray, which inspired Cantrell to design a 100-mile race; the race is not a tribute to Ray.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next section.

segments.title: Founding of the race in 1986 and format
segments.summary: Cantrell and Carl Hen (Raw Dog) hiked the park in 1985, were warned by a ranger, and then created the race. The first race was held over April Fool's weekend 1986 with 13 starters and no finishers. Early versions had three loops; the first finisher came after several attempts, and the elevation gain was initially misreported.

segments.title: Current race format: loops, elevation, time limit
segments.summary: The current race is officially 100 miles but is around 120 to 130 miles, with a 60-hour limit and about 60,000 feet of climb, with loops run alternating clockwise and counterclockwise, day and night, plus interloop rest periods and the sleep and pace math.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before discussing how to enter and run the race.

segments.title: Quitting, Fun Run, and the Barbecue Fall Classic
segments.summary: Runners who quit must walk back to the start-finish line, with no rescue. Finishing three loops is the Fun Run. A shorter Fall Classic of about 31 miles is held with about 35 to 40 participants.

segments.title: Application process and the race's personality
segments.summary: There is no website; applicants must find Cantrell's email and pay a 1.60 dollar non-refundable fee, often in two singles. Essays with odd prompts are used, and Cantrell's humor is described. Sacrificial 'human sacrifice' entrant mentioned, and first-timer and returning-runner gift traditions.

segments.title: Start of race and runner camaraderie
segments.summary: Runners wait for the conch blown at a random time, then the race starts when Cantrell lights a camel cigarette. Cantrell's rewards and the camaraderie among runners are discussed, along with the goal of pushing human limits.

segments.title: Navigation rules, no GPS, and book-page checkpoints
segments.summary: Runners have no GPS and only a basic map; some got lost. Proof of completing the route is ripping out pages from hidden books at checkpoints matching bib numbers, with stories of missing books and a runner finishing six seconds late.

segments.title: Taps, finish button, records, and first female finisher
segments.summary: Taps is played on a bugle for quitters by Dave Hen, and a Easy button marks finishes. The documentary finisher John Kelly is described. Official finisher counts, a record five finishers this year, and the first female finisher Jasmine Paris are covered, along with Cantrell's past comments about women.

segments.title: Finishers, records, and intelligence of runners
segments.summary: Jared Campbell as first four-time finisher, and hosts speculate about the high intelligence of participants. The current record by Brett Mahon is mentioned.

segments.title: John Fegyveresi Bad Water story
segments.summary: John Fegyveresi, an ultramarathoner, finished the Badwater ultramarathon in Death Valley and, delirious from sleep deprivation, ate a pint of ice cream and slept for hours afterward.

segments.title: Listener mail: lake versus pond
segments.summary: A listener from Minnesota explains lake versus pond distinctions: wave action and size, and Minnesota's 10-acre lake threshold versus Wisconsin's 2.5-acre. Hosts thank listener Mark and his sons and invite emails.
